The Harvard report contains communications from five authors :? By Dr. F. B. Mallory : "A contribution to the classification of tumours, based partly on his latest investigation of certain fibrils revealed by special methods of staining." By Dr. R. B. Greenough : "A paper on the nature of the cell inclusions of cancer," being a further contribution by the author on this subject. His conclusions, among others, are?

1. ?' That typical cell inclusions are practically constant in cancer of glandular origin." 2. "That these inclusions are presumably vacuoles." 3. "That the vacuoles are chiefly a phenomenon of cell secretion." 4. "That, in general, no reason exists for the interpretation of these appearances as of parasitic origin." By Drs. Vose and Howie: "A contribution on the effect of the Rontgen rays upon cancer." They conclude that the ar rays cannot be used strongly enough to destroy any but the shallowest tumour without producing an intractable burn. By Dr. E. H. Nichols : " Report of work in connection with the implantation of tissue and its relation to cancer."
His conclusions are as follows :

1. " Certain types of epithelium, both adult and foetal, can be experimentally removed from their normal position and implanted into another part of the same animal, and under those circumstances can maintain their * potentiality of growth,' retain their own peculiar character, and produce nodules analogous to dermoid cysts or more complicated teratomata." 2. " In no case has any epithelium of a highly differentiated function been seen to maintain its power of growth, or to proliferate." 3. "The 4 potentiality of growth' is greater in the case of foetal than it is in that of adult tissue."

4. "In no case has any infiltration of surrounding tissue of the transplanted epithelium been seen, nor any tendency to epithelial metastases." 5. "Certain foetal connective tissues (cartilage) can be transplanted in the same way as epithelial tissues, and retain their 'potentiality of growth.'" 6. "Transplanted foetal tissues do not reproduce the stage of development at which they are transplanted, but tend to reproduce the ultimate stage of their normal development." As regards the Buffalo report, the most significant article is one by Dr. G.

N. Calkins on "Cell inclusions in carcinoma." He finds that, in general, there are two main groups of inclusions in carcinoma?encapsulated and noncapsulated. Of the encapsulated inclusions he finds several forms which have been variously and erroneously interpreted as stages in the life-history of protozoa.

The non capsulated, he thinks, must be correctly interpreted before any hypothesis is advanced. Finally, he entertains the possibility at least that, even though few, the activity of the parasites may be causative of tumour growth. This report also contains a paper, by Dr. Gaylord, on the analogy between small-pox and cancer. It contains other papers besides these, many of which deal with the chemical aspect of the subject, and give evidence of much painstaking work which may in the future lead to important results. Dr. Roswell Park advocates the pursuing of the present laboratory investigations, and points out the advisability of physico-chemical study and the directing of attention to practical questions bearing on immunity. It is, however, noted with reference to these reports that comparatively little has been done, except in a negative way, towards the final solution of the main problems. For a few years previously she remarked that she was unable to read or write ; also that she could not count or write figures, while her hearing was quite good. There was no hemianopsia. There was, however, a slight verbal amnesia, but no motor impairment or impairment of the intellect.
She frequently strove to remember certain words, without being able to recall them.
She was conscious of this difficulty, and it caused her much annoyance.

She understood all that was said to her, and answered ?questions correctly ; also, if one related something to her she could repeat it correctly, although a slight paraphasia was observed. The patient recognised the objects and persons near her, and could name them. There was no paralysis of the limbs. Movements were equally well executed with either hand.

While the word-blindness was very marked, there was not complete alexia, inasmuch as the patient was able to distinguish the letters A, a, o, u, t, m. She was, however, unable to write a word properly, the letters so brought together conveying no meaning.
Two years after admission into hospital she took pneumonia, and died after four days' illness.

At the autopsy, examination of the brain revealed the following :?Atheromatous degeneration of the arteries. No change in the cortical substance of the right hemisphere. In the left an area of softening behind the ascending parietal convolution. The second and third frontal convolution, the island of Reil, and the ascending parietal convolution presented no change. The part which had undergone softening was the size of a five-franc piece ; it embraced the whole of the lower parietal lobe and the angular gyrus. The convolutions in the middle of the area of softening were yellow in colour and friable, and, towards the periphery, atrophied, and a flaky, yellow fluid flowed from openings at which rupture had taken place. The neighbouring convolutions, viz., the upper parietal and the posterior part of the first and second temporal, Avere atrophied and yellow in colour.

The slight paraphasia was ascribed to the lesions at the posterior part of the temporal convolutions. The word-blindness was considered to be due to the lesion in lower parietal lobe, while the agraphia was attributed to the involvement of the angular gyrus. This case shows that the centre associated with agraphia is not located at the base of the second left frontal convolution. No distinction could be made in this case between motor and sensory agraphia. Paraplegia in a Girl, aged 7-By l)r. Glorieux (Policlinique de Bruxtlle.s, 23, 1904 ;abstract from Deutsche-Medizinal-Zeituiuj, 13th March, 1905 : M. Loeb).?The patient had a fresh and rosy complexion, and was very intelligent for her years ; she had been badly trained, and was very much spoiled. There was complete paralysis of the lower limbs; the patellar reflexes were present, and the plantar reflexes weak ; Babinski's sign was absent. The sensibility of the skin was normal, or perhaps slightly diminished. The sphincter action was normal.

Passive movements appeared to cause pain. The father stated that since the commencement of her illness she complained of pain in the back and lower extremities when she was lifted or laid. She took her food excellently. She had suffered from scarlet fever for two months prior to this. The present illness was immediately preceded by two days of pyrexia and malaise. It was then found that the child was unable to use her limbs, this being ascribed to pain, which was felt pretty much over the whole body. Any attempt made to ascertain the electrical reactions had to be abandoned owing to the child becoming greatly excited and alarmed.

The physiognomy, the absence of motor and trophic changes, the presence of pain in the affected limbs and in the trunk (which might have been exaggerated or feigned), led the author to exclude poliomyelitis anterior, and to regard it as being of hysterical origin.

When l)r. Glorieux saw the patient eight days later, the patellar and tendo-hysterical. The examination of the sciatic, crural, and peroneal nerves bypressure manifestly caused pain, accordingly he came to the conclusion that it was a polyneuritis due to gastro-intoxication or the infection of scarlet fever. The galvanic current produced, at the head of the fibula, a slower contraction than in the normal condition.
The treatment consisted in the use of weak galvanic currents, gentle massage, passive and active movements. The author is hopeful of complete recovery in three months.
It is added that poliomyelitis anterior was excluded on account of the absence of atrophy in a pronounced degree met with in that disease.
